clue.text: Significance of what's coming from abroad.

definitions.meaning: goods brought into a country from overseas

explanation.surface: A musing on how much weight we give to things that arrive from overseas.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are standard: weight or meaning, and goods shipped in from another country.

clue.text: Flying, Amy died, alas — after sending this?

indicators.note: letters sent flying are scattered into a new order

parts.note: d is the abbreviation for died, as in genealogies
ay is an old exclamation of sorrow, like alas

explanation.surface: The aviator Amy Johnson died while flying; did she send a distress call first?
explanation.walkthrough: Amy Johnson was a famous British pioneer aviator who died in a crash in 1941, which gives the surface its point.
explanation.definitionFit: The international radio distress call is what a pilot sends before crashing, hence what she might have sent.

clue.text: Too serious back in romantic retreat, topless

indicators.note: the word for back sits inside the shortened retreat
losing its top means the first letter goes

parts.note: a love nest is a hideaway for lovers
the rear is the back

explanation.surface: A sober-minded person heads back to a love nest, where someone is going topless.
explanation.definitionFit: Excessively earnest describes someone overly solemn or intense, lacking any lightness.

clue.text: Slim, toothless person whose name one's forgotten.

parts.note: slim means thin
having no teeth leaves only gums, so the mouth is gummy

explanation.surface: Describing a skinny, gap-toothed person you just cannot put a name to.
explanation.definitionFit: A placeholder word, like whatsisname, used for someone or something you cannot name.

clue.text: Note misuse of "me" and "I", borders on careless one.

definitions.text: Note misuse of "me" and "I", borders on careless one

parts.note: sol (or soh) is the fifth note of the tonic sol-fa scale

indicators.note: a misuse of these letters puts them in the wrong order, so they are rearranged
the borders of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A grammar pedant complains that mixing up 'me' and 'I' is close to carelessness.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: saying 'between you and I' is exactly such a slip, so the misuse of pronouns is both the fodder and the meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A grammatical blunder such as confusing pronoun cases is the classic example of this kind of error.

clue.text: Evening broadcast covers pool bar opening.

indicators.note: the word for broadcast wraps around the other piece

parts.note: seed broadcast is scattered, or sown

indicators.note: barring the opening means the first letter is excluded

parts.note: a pool of money is a fund

explanation.surface: A TV programme in the evening shows the swimming pool bar opening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' suggests TV and 'pool bar' a poolside drinks bar, but they are SOWN and FUND without its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The time the sun sets marks the start of the evening, so the two are equivalent.

clue.text: Stable workers banking nothing very much.

indicators.note: the workers hold the nothing safely inside, as a bank holds money

parts.note: stable lads are the grooms who look after racehorses
O is the round figure for zero or nothing

explanation.surface: Stable hands save nothing at all, though they earn a lot.
explanation.definitionFit: A colloquial adverb meaning a great deal, as in 'thanks a lot'.

clue.text: Part of engine still left out.

indicators.note: the left letter is taken out of the word

parts.note: still means calm or tranquil

explanation.surface: An engine component is still missing from the left side.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotating projection on a shaft that opens engine valves, as in a camshaft.

clue.text: Associate party with brief enjoyment.

parts.note: a side is a party in a dispute or contest

indicators.note: a brief word is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: doing something for kicks is for enjoyment

explanation.surface: Joining a party for a short spell of fun.
explanation.definitionFit: A close companion or assistant who accompanies someone, a partner in their activities.

clue.text: Titan, excitable chief rejected.

parts.note: hyper means overexcited or highly strung

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so these letters are read backwards

parts.note: the chief is number one, written NO 1, taken as NOI

explanation.surface: A giant of a person, highly strung, has had their leader turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: Chief is No. 1; crosswords often read the digit 1 as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this figure was one of the Titans, the father of the sun god Helios.

clue.text: Fleet Street shunned by celebrity married lady

indicators.note: the celebrity word avoids the street abbreviation, so those letters are dropped from it

parts.note: a celebrity is a star
m is the abbreviation for married in genealogies and forms
Ada is a woman's name, a typical crossword 'lady'

explanation.surface: Fleet Street, home of the press, is avoided by a famous wedded woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleet Street' reads as the London newspaper district, but 'Fleet' is the definition and 'Street' a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A large fleet of warships, as in the Spanish one sent against England in 1588.

clue.text: Rogue ordered two grand.

parts.note: bade is a past tense of bid, meaning ordered or commanded
G is slang for a grand, a thousand pounds or dollars; two of them make GG

explanation.surface: A crook told someone to hand over two thousand pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for a bad character or scoundrel, someone who has turned out rotten.

clue.text: Leg hit is out.

parts.note: in cricket the leg side of the field is also called the on side
to strike is to hit

explanation.surface: A cricket report: the batsman's shot to leg ends with him dismissed.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket's leg side is also called the on side, the half of the field behind the batsman's legs.
explanation.definitionFit: Workers who are out are refusing to work in an industrial dispute, which is the meaning of the phrase.

clue.text: What, cobbled, might be used for a car.

definitions.text: What, cobbled, might be used for a car.

indicators.note: cobbled together means roughly assembled, so these letters are put together anew

explanation.surface: Asking what, once paved with cobblestones, a vehicle drives on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cobbled' rearranges the letters of USED FOR A CAR, and the whole clue describes the answer: a cobbled street is just such a surface used by cars.
explanation.definitionFit: The paved top layer of a street is what cars run on and may be laid with cobbles.

clue.text: Protest about Belgian town's sleepy state

parts.note: re is the Latin-derived word meaning about or concerning
Mons is a town in southern Belgium, famous for a First World War battle
a trance is a dazed, half-conscious state

explanation.surface: A complaint over the drowsy atmosphere of a provincial Belgian town.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal objection or forceful complaint, a word mainly met in political history.

clue.text: Debate party not in office.

parts.note: a thrash is British slang for a lively party
a party out of government is out of office

explanation.surface: A political party in opposition argues over its future.
explanation.walkthrough: A thrash is informal British English for a big party, not a political one.
explanation.definitionFit: To discuss a matter thoroughly until it is settled is a phrasal-verb sense of argue it through.

clue.text: Bliss, perhaps found in competition puzzle sharing quietly.

indicators.note: the two pieces share their joining letter, so it is written only once

parts.note: a poser is a puzzle or tricky question
p (piano) is the musical direction for quietly

explanation.surface: Delight found in solving a competition puzzle together, in silence.
explanation.walkthrough: COMP and POSER overlap on the shared P. Sir Arthur Bliss was an English composer and Master of the Queen's Music; 'perhaps' marks him as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Bliss wrote music, so he is one example of a music writer; 'perhaps' flags the example.

clue.text: With little love, they learn to adapt in empty lives?

definitions.text: With little love, they learn to adapt in empty lives?

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go inside the remaining shell of the next word
an emptied word keeps only its first and last letters

parts.note: love in tennis is zero, a small letter O

indicators.note: adapting the letters means reworking them into a new order

explanation.surface: Lonely people, short of affection, must learn to cope with hollow existences.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to adapt' rearranges O with THEY LEARN into ONELYHEART, which goes 'in' LS, all that is left of 'lives' when 'empty'. The whole clue also describes such people.
explanation.definitionFit: People seeking a partner through personal ads, the kind found on a newspaper's dating column.

clue.text: Worrying about small distance measured

indicators.note: the worrying word goes about, around, the small letter

parts.note: something eating you is worrying you
S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: Fretting over a short distance that has been measured out.
explanation.definitionFit: On maps and grids, the eastward distance from a reference line is measured as a coordinate.

clue.text: Mean clue, hard going? Editor keeping note!

indicators.note: the hard letter going means it is removed

parts.note: a hint is a clue
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

indicators.note: the editor abbreviation keeps the note letter inside it

parts.note: N is short for note, as in N.B.

explanation.surface: A solver grumbles that a clue is tough, while the editor takes note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' looks like an adjective (unkind clue) but is the verb, to have in mind.
explanation.definitionFit: To mean to do something is to plan or purpose it, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Move staff in periods of good fortune

indicators.note: the staff word sits inside the word for good times

parts.note: the ups of 'ups and downs' are good times
a staff is a walking stick

explanation.surface: Advice to carry a walking stick when things are going well.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is British slang meaning to pack up and move house.
explanation.definitionFit: A British idiom for relocating, gathering up your belongings and leaving for somewhere new.

clue.text: Divided with a hundred over.

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
what is over is left, remaining

explanation.surface: A cricket score: split, with a century already reached.
explanation.definitionFit: Split or cut in two, as a cleft chin or a cloven hoof.

clue.text: Ply a street in London.

definitions.meaning: a ply is one twisted thread of yarn or rope
a major street in central London running from Trafalgar Square towards the City

explanation.surface: An instruction to work a particular London thoroughfare, as a cabbie or street trader might.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ply' looks like a verb, as in plying a trade, but here it is the noun for a thread.
explanation.definitionFit: A single thread twisted into rope is a ply, and the London street is a famous proper name.

clue.text: Fly first-class twice — not second class — and back.

indicators.note: going back means the letters are read in reverse
the shortened word is written two times over
not having the second-class letter means it is removed

parts.note: the best is first-class quality
B is the grade for second class, after A

explanation.surface: Instructions for travel: fly first class both ways, never second, out and return.
explanation.walkthrough: BEST without B is EST; 'twice' makes ESTEST, and 'back' turns it round. 'Fly' looks like a verb about travel but is the insect.
explanation.definitionFit: This African biting insect is a fly that spreads sleeping sickness.

clue.text: Busy, maybe going into rising inheritance tax.

indicators.note: in a down entry rising means read from bottom to top, backwards
the letters go into the words, spanning the gap between them

explanation.surface: Someone occupied with filling in a form for inheritance tax that keeps going up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Busy' is British slang for a police detective; 'maybe' marks it as an example. CET straddles 'inheritance tax' and is read upward.
explanation.definitionFit: A short informal word for a detective, of whom a busy is one slang example.

clue.text: Huge admirer shows marriage promise after a time.

parts.note: 'I do' is the vow spoken at a wedding
later means after some time has passed

explanation.surface: A devoted fan finally proposes and makes the wedding vow eventually.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who worships a person or image, an idol-worshipper, is an extreme devotee.

clue.text: Parking car I get careless — ticket!

parts.note: P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

indicators.note: carelessly arranged letters fall into a muddled order

explanation.surface: A driver complains of getting sloppy with parking and being fined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ticket' suggests a parking fine but means the label showing what something costs.
explanation.definitionFit: A ticket attached to goods shows their cost, which is exactly a label with the amount on it.

clue.text: Hot tip in tax.

indicators.note: the word for tip goes inside the word for tax

parts.note: to try is to tax or strain, as in trying someone's patience
a tip is an end, as of a pencil

explanation.surface: A financial tip-off about where tax is heading.
explanation.definitionFit: Hot in the sense of fashionable or currently popular, the latest thing.
